channel.title: ThinkWork Blog
channel.description: Practitioner writing on sales enablement, coaching and the mastery layer.

item.title: Your AI Notetaker Isn't Taking Notes. It's Building a Model of How Your Reps Sell.
item.description: Every call your AI notetaker logs is a training signal. Most sales orgs have no idea what they're teaching it.

item.title: You Built a Structured Interview Scorecard. Your Hiring Managers Aren't Using It.
item.description: Structured interviews only work if the rubric survives contact with a strong personality in the room. Most don't.

item.title: Your Enablement Content Audit Is Asking the Wrong Question
item.description: Most content audits measure what exists and what's used. Neither tells you whether the content actually moves a skill.

item.title: What Your AI Scorecard Cannot See From a Transcript
item.description: Transcripts capture words. Scores require judgement. The gap between the two is where your AI scoring layer is quietly getting it wrong.

item.title: Accelerator Cliffs Are a Behavioural Tax on Your Best Reps
item.description: The accelerator structure every comp plan brags about is quietly teaching your top performers to sandbag Q4.

item.title: Pipeline Coverage Is a Lagging Indicator Dressed Up as a Leading One
item.description: 3x coverage feels like safety. It isn't. By the time your coverage ratio looks healthy, the deals inside it are already decaying.

item.title: Most Outbound Cadences Are Too Short. Here's What the Drop-Off Data Actually Shows.
item.description: Teams cap cadences at 5-7 touches because it feels polite. The conversion data says they're stopping just before it gets interesting.

item.title: The Discovery Call That Ran 90 Minutes Was Probably a Failure
item.description: Call length is how reps signal effort to their manager. It has almost nothing to do with how much they actually learned.

item.title: Your Methodology Rollout Didn't Fail at Launch. It Failed at Month Two.
item.description: SKO energy masks a 60-day cliff. Here's what the data from four rollouts actually shows about where adoption dies.

item.title: The Manager Who Coaches Everyone Equally Is Actually Coaching Nobody
item.description: Equal coaching time feels fair. It is also one of the most reliable ways to waste it. Here's what the data actually suggests.

item.title: Week One of Onboarding Is Mostly Wasted. Here's the Evidence.
item.description: What new reps actually do in their first five days, what any of it predicts, and where the real ramp damage gets baked in.

item.title: The 90-Day Ramp Curriculum, Ranked by What Actually Predicts Quota Attainment
item.description: Most onboarding curricula run product training first and live calls last. What actually correlates with hitting quota says do the opposite.

item.title: Ramp Time Is the Wrong Metric. Competency-Tier Attainment Predicts Retention.
item.description: Days-to-first-deal looks precise. It predicts almost nothing about whether a rep is still carrying quota twelve months later.

item.title: How to Build a Ramp Plan Around Skill Tiers Instead of Calendar Days
item.description: The 30/60/90 template assumes every rep learns at the same speed. Gating the plan on skill tiers instead of dates fixes the two failure modes calendar plans can't.

item.title: Sales Ramp Time Benchmarks by Industry Are Mostly Noise. Here's What They Leave Out.
item.description: The commonly-quoted average ramp time gets cited without the denominator that would make it mean anything.

item.title: Eight Onboarding Certification Gates, Ranked by How Easy They Are to Fake
item.description: A new rep can pass a product quiz, ace a scripted role-play, and still fall apart on their first real discovery call. Most certification gates measure the wrong thing.

item.title: I Read Three SaaS Onboarding Decks Cover to Cover. None of Them Taught Discovery.
item.description: Ninety slides on product, pricing and objection scripts. Zero slides on how to ask a question that changes the deal.

item.title: What 'Fully Ramped' Actually Means, and Why Every Team Defines It Differently
item.description: Ask five sales leaders what 'ramped' means and you'll get five different thresholds, none of them written down anywhere.

item.title: What Slow Rampers Actually Have in Common (It Isn't Aptitude)
item.description: Two reps hired the same week, same background, same territory. One ramped in six weeks. One took five months. The gap wasn't talent.

item.title: How to Run Call-Shadowing So New Reps Learn Something Instead of Just Listening
item.description: Most shadowing programs are new reps taking notes on autopilot. A structured observation rubric turns the same hours into measurable skill transfer.

item.title: What to Actually Ask For in Your First 30 Days as a New Rep
item.description: Most new reps wait to be told what to do. The ones who ramp fastest ask for three specific things their manager won't offer by default.

item.title: Office Hours: The Ramp Questions Enablement Leaders Keep Asking Me
item.description: Same six questions, every quarter, from every enablement leader building a ramp program. Straight answers to all of them.

item.title: Stop Building Onboarding by Reverse-Engineering Your Best Rep
item.description: Shadowing your top performer feels like the obvious way to build a curriculum. It usually teaches new hires someone else's compensations, not the skill underneath them.

item.title: Your 1:1s Are Status Meetings Wearing a Coaching Costume
item.description: If the average manager 1:1 got minuted, most of it would read as a pipeline update. That's not coaching, it's admin with a whiteboard.

item.title: How to Run a 20-Minute 1:1 That's Actually Coaching, Not a Pipeline Check-In
item.description: One skill, one observed moment, one named gap, one practice rep. Here's the structure that keeps a 1:1 from sliding into deal triage.

item.title: Six Coaching Habits Sales Managers Swear By, Ranked by Whether They Move Any Skill at All
item.description: Call shadowing, deal reviews, scorecards, roleplay, peer coaching, and 'great job' energy, ranked from placebo to load-bearing.

item.title: We Scored 40,000 Coaching Moments Against 54 Competencies. Managers Coach Five of Them and Ignore the Rest.
item.description: Objection handling gets coached to death. Discovery depth and negotiation barely get mentioned. Here's where manager attention actually goes.

item.title: How to Run a Coaching Calibration Session So Two Managers Stop Grading the Same Call Differently
item.description: Blind-grade the same call, compare scores, argue about the gaps, anchor the rubric. Skip this and your 'coaching program' is just manager opinion with a template.

item.title: Promoting Your Best Rep to Manager Is a Skill Transplant, and the Body Usually Rejects It
item.description: The instincts that make someone a killer at execution are not the instincts that make someone good at diagnosing why someone else can't execute.

item.title: We Graded 12 Manager 1:1 Recordings Against a Coaching Rubric. Here's What Separated the Top Two.
item.description: Not tone. Not energy. Not rapport. The top two did one specific thing the other ten never did once.

item.title: The Five Sales Feedback Phrases That Teach a Rep Nothing, Ranked by How Often Managers Say Them Anyway
item.description: 'Great job,' 'just be more confident,' 'nice energy': ranked from mildly useless to actively harmful, with what to say instead of each.

item.title: What 'Competency-Based Coaching' Actually Means, and Why Most Coaching Programs Never Get There
item.description: Not a values poster. Not a scorecard bolted onto a CRM. A working definition, and the three things that have to be true before you can claim it.

item.title: What Happened When We Made Managers Score Their Own 1:1s Before We Scored Them
item.description: The self-scores and the external scores didn't just differ: they diverged in a consistent direction, and that direction told us more than the scores themselves.

item.title: The Manager Skill Nobody Puts on a Job Description: Diagnosing Before Prescribing
item.description: Every job description for 'sales manager' lists coaching as a bullet point. None of them explain that the actual skill is diagnosis: and diagnosis is learnable in a specific, trainable way.

item.title: We Asked Sales Leaders How They Know Their Managers Can Actually Coach. Most Didn't Have an Answer.
item.description: 'They've been doing it ten years' is not a measurement. Composite notes from conversations with revenue leaders on the question most of them had never been asked directly.

item.title: MEDDPICC Isn't a Sales Methodology. It's a Forecasting Filter.
item.description: Every methodology fight assumes MEDDPICC and Challenger are competing for the same job. They aren't, and confusing a scoring rubric for a conversation script is why so many "MEDDPICC teams" still can't run discovery.

item.title: SPIN, Challenger, Sandler: Three Different Answers to 'What Do I Say Next'
item.description: The war over "which methodology" usually skips a more useful question: which moment in the call is each one actually built for. Here's the honest division of labor.

item.title: Ranked: MEDDPICC, Challenger, SPIN, and Sandler by How Hard They Are to Run Live
item.description: Forget adoption stats and LinkedIn endorsements. Ranked by what it actually takes to run each framework live, on a call, under pressure, with a verdict most enablement decks won't say out loud.

item.title: How to Run MEDDPICC Discovery Without Sounding Like a Checklist
item.description: MEDDPICC gets a bad name because it gets asked badly. A field-by-field rework of the checklist into questions a human would actually say out loud.

item.title: We Scored 500 Discovery Calls Against Four Sales Methodologies. Here's What Reps Actually Used.
item.description: We pulled the assessment data on 500 real discovery calls scored against four named frameworks. The gap between the deck and the transcript is bigger, and more consistent, than most VPs of Sales want to hear.

item.title: The Champion Criterion Is Where MEDDPICC Deals Actually Die: A Test for Fake Champions
item.description: "Champion" is the one MEDDPICC letter nobody verifies, it just gets typed in after a nice call. Here's the test that catches the ones who'll disappear the second the deal gets hard.

item.title: Challenger's 'Teach, Tailor, Take Control': Most Teams Only Ever Install the First Word
item.description: Everyone can recite "Teach, Tailor, Take Control." Almost nobody's team can do the second and third word. Here's why the muscle never gets built.

item.title: Sandler's Pain Funnel Is a Negotiation Skill Wearing a Discovery Costume
item.description: Sandler gets filed under "discovery framework." It's really a lesson in tolerating silence and letting pressure do the qualifying for you, and teaching it as questions instead of composure is why it doesn't stick.

item.title: Your Methodology Switch Isn't the Problem. Your Ramp Program Is.
item.description: Before you blame the framework for the miss, check the onboarding curriculum. Most methodology switches are a company re-labeling a problem it never actually fixed.

item.title: Ranked: Which Sales Methodology Fits Your GTM Motion, From Transactional to Enterprise
item.description: MEDDPICC is not GTM-agnostic and nobody says so out loud. A blunt map of which framework fits which motion, and which one will actively slow you down.

item.title: What Mastering MEDDPICC Actually Does for Your Career, Beyond the CRM Fields
item.description: Mastering a qualification framework isn't a compliance exercise for your CRM. It's the difference between "hit quota" and "got promoted", here's the actual mechanism.

item.title: Field Notes: Four Teams, Four Methodologies, One Identical Failure
item.description: Four teams, four different named methodologies, four audits. Same exact failure every time, and it had nothing to do with which framework was on the wall.

item.title: The 9 Discovery Questions That Actually Predict Deal Outcomes (And the 40 That Don't)
item.description: A ranked breakdown of which discovery questions actually correlate with progressed and won deals, and why most 'best questions' lists are recycled folklore.

item.title: MEDDIC Doesn't Fail on Process. It Fails on 'Decision Criteria.'
item.description: Every MEDDIC post-mortem blames a skipped step. The real failure point is one under-coached field that almost nobody actually trains.

item.title: How to Run Discovery When the Buyer Already Picked a Vendor in Their Head
item.description: A concrete sequence for reopening a 'decided' buyer's evaluation without sounding like you're relitigating their judgment.
